ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Psychology Ethics Committee at the University of Aberdeen (Worktribe ID 815096).
Participants were recruited from the University of Aberdeen School of Psychology participant pool and through local advertisements and received either course credit or financial compensation.
All participants provided informed consent before taking part and were fully debriefed following their final session.
Each participant completed one cTBS, one iTBS, and one sham stimulation session.
Participants were blind to stimulation condition and were monitored for discomfort and adverse events during and after stimulation.
Immediately after stimulation, participants completed the production-effect task.
Participants were instructed to try to remember all words for a memory test that would follow.
After the recognition phase in the third session, participants completed the Lexical Test for Advanced Learners of English (LexTALE; Lemhöfer and Broersma, 2012), a brief test of English proficiency.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> No participants were excluded.

> Participants were recruited from the University of Aberdeen School of Psychology participant pool and through local advertisements and received either course credit or financial compensation.

> All participants provided informed consent before taking part and were fully debriefed following their final session.

> Each participant completed one cTBS, one iTBS, and one sham stimulation session.

> Participants were blind to stimulation condition and were monitored for discomfort and adverse events during and after stimulation.

> Immediately after stimulation, participants completed the production-effect task.

> Participants were instructed to try to remember all words for a memory test that would follow.

> After the recognition phase in the third session, participants completed the Lexical Test for Advanced Learners of English (LexTALE; Lemhöfer and Broersma, 2012), a brief test of English proficiency.

> To estimate the variability of the AUC values and compare conditions, a bootstrap procedure with replacement was used: on each of 10,000 iterations, participants were resampled with replacement while preserving the within-participant dependency between the aloud and silent conditions, and AUC values were recomputed.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The target sample size was determined using a simulation-based power analysis for a three-level repeated-measures comparison, implemented in R using the 'MASS' package (Venables & Ripley, 2013). The simulation assumed a target power level of 0.90, two-sided alpha level of 0.05, rho of 0.50, and a standardised mean difference of d = 0.52, based on reported effects of TMS on verbal memory accuracy (Osaka et al., 2007). The analysis indicated that 40 complete datasets were required.

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect.
This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding.

Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).
In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC.
They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent thetaburst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation.
Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements.
There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently.
Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS.

Exploratory receiver-operatingcharacteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud.
Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words.

These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, DLPFC AND THE PRODUCTION EFFECT 3 consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

Reading a word aloud at study reliably improves subsequent memory for that word relative to reading it silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect (Hopkins & Edwards, 1972; MacLeod et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Reading a word aloud at study reliably improves subsequent memory for that word relative to reading it silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hopkins & Edwards, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">MacLeod et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This memory advantage extends across materials, memory tests, and forms of production (Fawcett, 2013; Forrin et al., 2012; MacLeod & Bodner, 2017; Zormpa et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This memory advantage extends across materials, memory tests, and forms of production <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fawcett, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Forrin et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">MacLeod & Bodner, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Zormpa et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A prominent explanation is that production makes an item distinctive in memory: speaking adds auditory, articulatory, and somatosensory features that can provide evidence of prior study (Bailey et al., 2021; MacLeod et al., 2010).
text.formatted: A prominent explanation is that production makes an item distinctive in memory: speaking adds auditory, articulatory, and somatosensory features that can provide evidence of prior study <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bailey et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">MacLeod et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These features are particularly useful in mixed-list designs, where aloud and silent words are studied together (Ozubko & MacLeod, 2010).
text.formatted: These features are particularly useful in mixed-list designs, where aloud and silent words are studied together <ref type="bibr">(Ozubko & MacLeod, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from neuroimaging and psychophysiology links the production benefit to both sensorimotor processing and preparation to speak.
Activity in auditory, motor, and somatosensory regions during encoding is associated with subsequent recollection of aloud words (Bailey et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Activity in auditory, motor, and somatosensory regions during encoding is associated with subsequent recollection of aloud words <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bailey et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Preparing to read aloud also elicits greater pupil dilation and larger cue-evoked P300 responses than preparing to read silently (Fawcett et al., 2026a; Hassall et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Preparing to read aloud also elicits greater pupil dilation and larger cue-evoked P300 responses than preparing to read silently <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fawcett et al., 2026a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hassall et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Preparing to read a word aloud can even improve memory relative to silent reading when the anticipated signal to speak never appears (Fawcett et al., 2026b).
text.formatted: Preparing to read a word aloud can even improve memory relative to silent reading when the anticipated signal to speak never appears <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fawcett et al., 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, processes preceding vocalisation may contribute to the memory benefit alongside the sensorimotor information generated by speaking.

These findings are consistent with a contribution from cognitive control, defined here as the use of goals and task rules to guide processing and behaviour (Friedman & Robbins, 2022; Miller & Cohen, 2001).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with a contribution from cognitive control, defined here as the use of goals and task rules to guide processing and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Friedman & Robbins, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Miller & Cohen, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In a mixed-list task, participants must select the instructed reading mode, with aloud trials additionally requiring preparation and coordination of a vocal response.
Control processes may help prioritise production-related information and incorporate it into the memory representation of the word.
This proposal complements the distinctiveness explanation by identifying control processes that could support the encoding and use of distinctive features.
However, existing behavioural and physiological evidence does not establish whether a neural system supporting cognitive control causally contributes to the production effect.

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) provides a plausible neural substrate for a control contribution to the production effect because of its role in maintaining task goals and biasing processing towards relevant representations and actions (Badre & Nee, 2018; Miller & Cohen, 2001).
text.formatted: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) provides a plausible neural substrate for a control contribution to the production effect because of its role in maintaining task goals and biasing processing towards relevant representations and actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Badre & Nee, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Miller & Cohen, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: It also supports the organisation of information during encoding and the evaluation of retrieved information (Blumenfeld & Ranganath, 2007; Dobbins et al., 2002; Murray & Ranganath, 2007).

text.text: In production-based tasks, these functions could support the encoding of production-related features and their subsequent use as evidence that a word was studied.
If DLPFC-supported control helps confer the memory advantage of speaking, perturbing this region should alter the aloud-silent memory difference.

We tested this proposal in a preregistered within-participant study crossing encoding condition (aloud, silent) with bilateral DLPFC stimulation (continuous theta-burst stimulation [cTBS], intermittent theta-burst stimulation [iTBS], sham).

text.text: We predicted that aloud items would be recognised more accurately and rapidly, with greater confidence and recollection (H1), and that iTBS would increase whereas cTBS would reduce this advantage relative to sham (H2).
Forty adult participants (22 female, 17 male, and 1 non-binary), aged 18-41 years (M = 22.8, SD = 3.88) completed three experimental sessions and were included in the analyses.
No participants were excluded.
Participants were recruited from the University of Aberdeen School of Psychology participant pool and through local advertisements and received either course credit or financial compensation.
Eligibility required self-reported proficiency in English and fulfilment of TMS safety criteria, assessed with a TMS screening questionnaire.
Individuals were not eligible to participate if they reported contraindications for TMS, including a personal or family history of seizures or epilepsy, or other neurological conditions.
The study was approved by the Psychology Ethics Committee at the University of Aberdeen (Worktribe ID 815096).
All participants provided informed consent before taking part and were fully debriefed following their final session.
The target sample size was determined using a simulation-based power analysis for a three-level repeated-measures comparison, implemented in R using the 'MASS' package (Venables & Ripley, 2013).

text.text: Active motor threshold (AMT) measurement.
Each participant's AMT was measured using surface electromyography at the start of their first session.

After skin preparation, surface electrodes were placed over the right first dorsal interosseous (FDI) muscle, with the active electrode over the muscle belly, the reference electrode on the index finger, and the ground electrode on the dorsum of the hand.

The coil was adjusted to identify the motor hotspot, and stimulation intensity was varied adaptively.
AMT was defined as the lowest stimulator output that elicited motorevoked potentials (MEPs) of at least 150 μV peak-to-peak amplitude in at least three of five consecutive trials.

Production Effect Task Encoding phase.
Immediately after stimulation, participants completed the production-effect task.
Inquisit Lab 6 software (Millisecond, Seattle, USA) was used for stimulus presentation.
The encoding phase contained 80 trials: 40 words presented in blue, which participants read aloud, and 40 words presented in white, which participants read silently.
Stimuli were presented on a black background.
Each word was displayed for 2000 ms, followed by a 500 ms inter-trial interval, in a random order for each participant in each session.
Participants were instructed to try to remember all words for a memory test that would follow.
The recognition phase contained 160 trials -the 80 studied words and 80 new words-all presented in yellow, in a unique random test order.
For each word, participants first made an old/new recognition judgement by pressing 'Y' for old or 'N' for new.
They then rated their confidence from 1 (not sure at all) to 4 (very sure).

For words judged as old, participants indicated whether they recollected any specific detail from encoding episode, such as the word's colour or whether it had been spoken, by responding 'Y' for yes or 'N' for no.
All recognition phase responses were self-paced.

After the recognition phase in the third session, participants completed the Lexical Test for Advanced Learners of English (LexTALE; Lemhöfer and Broersma, 2012), a brief test of English proficiency.

The experiment used a 3 × 2 within-participant design with stimulation condition (sham, cTBS, iTBS) and encoding condition (aloud, silent) as factors.
Stimulation condition varied between sessions, with one condition administered per session and session order counterbalanced across participants; encoding condition varied within each session.
Dependent measures included recognition accuracy, response time, confidence, and recollection.
All analyses were conducted in R with a significance criterion of α = .05.
Confirmatory analyses followed the preregistered analysis plan and were implemented with the 'rstatix' package.
For all repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs), sphericity was assessed with Mauchly's test, and uncorrected degrees of freedom are reported where sphericity held.
Preregistered tests of the production effect and its modulation.

To test for H1, i.e., the presence of a production effect, we examined the effect of encoding condition (aloud vs silent) on each of four memory measures-recognition accuracy (hit rate) for old words, response time for correctly recognised old items, confidence, and recollection-using pairedsamples t-tests that collapsed across stimulation condition.
Effect sizes are reported as dz.

For response-time analyses, we retained only correctly recognised old-item trials and excluded individual trials with latencies more than 3 SD above or below the grand mean of those trials before computing participant-level means, limiting the influence of atypically fast or slow responses that were unlikely to reflect engaged task performance.
To test for H2, i.e., the role of the DLPFC in the production effect, we first computed within-participant difference scores in each stimulation condition.

Difference scores were calculated as aloud minus silent for recognition accuracy (hit rates), confidence, and recollection, and as silent minus aloud for response time, such that positive scores consistently indicated an advantage for aloud items.
For each measure, these scores were submitted to a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with stimulation condition (sham, cTBS, and iTBS) as the within-participant factor.

Recognition accuracy (hit rate) was designated the primary outcome for H2 because it provides the most direct behavioural index of recognition success and was the measure on which the a priori sample size calculation was based (Osaka et al., 2007).

Exploratory robustness and decomposition analyses.
Exploratory follow-up analyses were then used to assess the robustness of the primary accuracy finding.

To characterise how the stimulation-related change in the production effect was distributed across encoding conditions, participant-level old-word hit rates were analysed using a 3 (stimulation: sham, cTBS, iTBS) × 2 (encoding: aloud, silent) repeated-measures ANOVA.
The stimulation × encoding interaction is algebraically equivalent to the one-way stimulation effect on the corresponding aloud-minus-silent difference scores.
Pairwise comparisons were Holm-corrected pairwise across the six simple effect pairwise contrasts.
We also assessed whether the effects of TMS on recognition accuracy could reflect a speed-accuracy trade-off in an exploratory analysis.
Within each stimulation × encoding condition, we correlated old-word recognition accuracy (hit rate) with mean response time.
In addition, within each stimulation condition, we correlated the magnitude of the accuracy production effect (aloud minus silent) with the magnitude of the response-time production effect.
Correlations were computed as Pearson's r, with Spearman's rho reported as a sensitivity analysis, and Bonferroni-corrected p values within each family of comparisons.

To test whether stimulation produced a general change in recognition responding, performance on new words-rejection rate, confidence, response time, and false-alarm recollection-was analysed using a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with stimulation condition as the within-participant factor.
New-word response times were computed on correct rejections only, following the hits-only definition used for old words.

Exploratory receiver-operatingcharacteristic (ROC) analyses were used to distinguish mnemonic discriminability from response criterion.

ROC curves were constructed for each condition by combining the old/new decision and four-point confidence rating were combined into an eight-category ordered response scale ranging from a high-confidence "new" response to a high-confidence "old" response.
For each stimulation and encoding condition, cumulative hit and false-alarm rates were calculated across successive criteria to construct the empirical ROC.

text.text: To examine whether TMS altered the magnitude of the production effect, we fit a series of nested UVSD models in which the increase in discriminability associated with producing items aloud rather than silently (i.e., the production effect) was constrained to be identical across stimulation conditions.
Because discriminability in the UVSD model is indexed by da, these constraints were imposed directly on the production-related change in da.
We first constrained the production effect to be equal between the cTBS and sham conditions.
This constraint significantly worsened model fit, χ²(7) = 7.52, Δχ²(1) = 5.30, p = .021, indicating that the production effect differed reliably between these stimulation conditions.
We next constrained the production effect to be equal between the iTBS and sham conditions.

In contrast, this constraint did not significantly worsen model fit, χ²(7) = 2.28, Δχ²(1) = 0.06, p = .812, indicating that the production effect was statistically comparable under iTBS and sham stimulation.

These model-based analyses thus closely mirrored the nonparametric ROC analyses: cTBS selectively attenuated the production effect relative to sham stimulation, while iTBS produced no detectable change in the magnitude of the production advantage relative to sham.
The present study tested using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) whether the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) causally contributes to the production effect in recognition memory.

Reading words aloud produced the expected advantage over silent reading: aloud items had higher hit rates, were recognised more rapidly and confidently, and were more often accompanied by reported recollection.
Crucially, continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) reduced the magnitude of the production effect relative to both sham and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS).

Receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) analyses provided converging evidence for a smaller production advantage in aloud vs silent word discriminability following cTBS relative to sham stimulation.

Finally, stimulation did not reliably alter responses to new words, and the accuracy effects were not accompanied by evidence of a speed-accuracy trade-off, arguing against a general shift in recognition responding or response strategy.
Taken together, these findings provide the first causal evidence that DLPFC-targeted stimulation can alter the relative memory advantage conferred by speaking.
DLPFCsupported cognitive control may contribute to the production effect by shaping how production-related information is selected during encoding and used during recognition.

The overall advantage for aloud items across accuracy, response time, confidence, and reported recollection replicates previous findings (Kelly et al., 2022; MacLeod et al., 2010; Ozubko et al., 2012).

Distinctiveness provides a useful framework for interpreting this advantage: speaking generates auditory, articulatory, and somatosensory information that can help distinguish studied items from new items (Bailey et al., 2021; MacLeod et al., 2010; Saint-Aubin et al., 2021).

DLPFC-supported control may help determine how production-related information becomes available and useful for remembering.

We therefore propose complementary roles of production and cognitive control in working toward an integrative account of the production effect: production supplies potentially distinctive information, while control helps prioritise and use that information.
During mixed-list encoding, participants must interpret each trial cue (e.g., word colour) and select the instructed reading mode (e.g., reading aloud vs silently).
Aloud trials additionally require participants to prepare and execute a vocal response, check its accuracy, and process its auditory consequences.

The DLPFC may maintain the current task rule and coordinate these operations, increasing the likelihood that production-related features are incorporated into the representation of the word (Badre & Nee, 2018; Friedman & Robbins, 2022; Miller & Cohen, 2001).

text.text: Perturbing this contribution could make the resulting memories for aloud and silent items less differentiated.
At recognition, DLPFC-supported control might instead, or additionally, help evaluate production-related features as evidence that an item was studied.
This interpretation also connects the present results to evidence that productionrelated processing begins before vocalisation.

text.text: Preparation can therefore contribute to the memory benefit alongside the sensory and motor consequences of speaking.
The present stimulation findings extend this evidence by implicating a neural system that could support the selection and coordination of productionrelated processing.
While production supplies additional sensorimotor features, cognitive control may influence how strongly those features are selected, bound to the studied word, or used at recognition.
The persistence of a production effect following cTBS is consistent with this integrated account.
Sensorimotor information remained available, but its mnemonic influence may have been weakened when the DLPFC contribution was perturbed.

The ROC and UVSD findings help clarify the behavioural effect because hit rates alone can vary with response criterion (Brady et al., 2023; Hautus et al., 2021; Wixted, 2023. The reduced cTBS-sham difference in discriminability suggests that the primary accuracy result reflected a change in mnemonic sensitivity rather than simply a greater or lesser tendency to respond "old", although these model-based analyses were exploratory.

text.text: The absence of reliable stimulation effects on new-word responses and the lack of a speedaccuracy trade-off further argue against a global change in response strategy or general slowing.
The predicted reduction in the production effect following cTBS was accompanied by no detectable enhancement following iTBS.

Although cTBS and iTBS are commonly associated with decreased and increased motor-cortical excitability, respectively, these protocols do not guarantee opposing effects in the prefrontal cortex, as TBS responses vary substantially across individuals (Chung et al., 2019; Lowe & Hall, 2018; Suppa et al., 2016).

text.text: The iTBS result could reflect the lack of reliable physiological effect on DLPFC function, a physiological change without a corresponding behavioural benefit, or heterogeneous effects that were obscured at the group level.

The current task's substantial memory and responseselection demands may also have resulted in relevant control processes being strongly recruited under sham stimulation, leaving limited scope for further enhancement under iTBS.
Several future research questions remain.

While the present study provides causal evidence that the DLPFC contributes to the production effect, it remains to be established whether this contribution generalises to other populations, forms of production, or memory tests such as free recall.
Additionally, behavioural measures alone cannot identify the exact operation affected by DLPFC stimulation.

Candidate mechanisms include maintaining task rules, suppressing competing responses, selecting production-related features, binding those features to the word, and/or monitoring evidence at retrieval.

The present pattern of results provides reason to predict potentially stronger DLPFC contributions at encoding: cTBS attenuated memory for studied items without affecting responses to new words, arguing against a nonspecific effect on recognition decisions or response criterion and suggesting that disruption may instead have altered processes involved in forming production-related memory traces.
Future studies using temporally specific stimulation during encoding and retrieval could directly distinguish these possibilities.

Combining TMS with pupillometry or EEG could also be used to determine whether DLPFC perturbation attenuates the preparatory signals previously associated with intended production, thereby providing converging evidence for an encoding stage contribution.
In sum, DLPFC-targeted cTBS reduced the recognition advantage for words read aloud, linking the production effect to neural processes implicated in cognitive control.
The findings support the proposal that production supplies distinctive information whose mnemonic value depends partly on how that information is prioritised and used.
While production may supply features that can distinguish an item in memory, cognitive control may help determine how strongly those features are selected, bound, or used during the memory episode.
The present study identifies the DLPFC as one potential contributor to that interaction.
Thus, the advantage of saying a word aloud is not simply a stronger trace left behind by speaking-it is a trace whose mnemonic consequences are partly shaped by prefrontal control.
